endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: This includes evaluating risk modifiers such as population sensitivity, disparity risk, data provenance verifiability (with models whose training data provenance is unknown or unverifiable carrying a higher default risk regardless of intended use), and the sufficiency of information about the solution’s training data.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether assigning higher default risk to AI with unknown training-data provenance or thin vendor documentation changes detection of bias, failure modes, or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on a single governance framework endorsement from CHAI, which states the practice as a "should."

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard it targets. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The supporting basis consists of expert consensus in one framework, which indicates what reviewers believe is prudent but does not show that the practice works.

The CHAI playbook lists data provenance verifiability as a risk modifier and states that models with unknown or unverifiable provenance carry higher default risk regardless of intended use. This is voluntary guidance from one source. The supplied materials include no statute, rule, or agency guidance that requires this weighting.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare risk-review processes that raise default risk for undocumented or unverifiable models with processes that do not. Outcomes should include the rate at which bias or performance failures are found before deployment, time and staff cost per review, and downstream patient harm. Studies documenting how often vendor opacity has concealed failure modes would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on its effect in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The CHAI framework names population sensitivity and disparity risk as modifiers, but whether provenance-based risk weighting protects these groups remains untested.
